justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly upward-drifting baseline from what I assumed was a current price near $205–206. At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the prevailing price with only a small drift component, since markets tend to exhibit mean-reversion over very short windows and any single session is unlikely to move dramatically absent a specific catalyst. For the one-week estimate, I applied a slightly larger drift assumption consistent with a mildly bullish near-term trend, while still keeping the estimate close to current levels since weekly moves in broad indices or individual securities rarely deviate sharply from a random walk without fundamental news. At the one-month horizon, I incorporated a slightly higher drift to reflect the compounding of daily expected returns over roughly 21 trading days, arriving at a modest appreciation from current levels.

The confidence interval widths were primarily driven by historical volatility assumptions scaled to each time horizon. For the one-day interval, I used a relatively tight band because daily realized volatility, even in moderately volatile assets, tends to keep 90% of outcomes within a few percentage points of the starting price. As the horizon extends to one week and especially one month, uncertainty compounds roughly with the square root of time, which explains why the one-month interval is considerably wider than the one-day interval. I also factored in the possibility of volatility clustering — the idea that calm periods can be interrupted by sudden spikes — which added a small additional margin to the longer-horizon intervals.

There are several risks that could push outcomes well outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden macroeconomic shock — such as an unexpected central bank policy shift, a deterioration in credit markets, a geopolitical escalation, or a disappointing earnings or economic data release — could produce a sharp sell-off that breaches the lower bound of even the one-month interval. On the upside, a strong positive catalyst like a surprise earnings beat, a dovish policy pivot, or a broader risk-on rally could push prices beyond my upper bounds. My stated intervals assume relatively normal market conditions and do not fully account for fat-tailed events or sudden liquidity crises, which are low-probability but high-impact scenarios that any honest forecast should acknowledge as genuine tail risks.
